source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Are Large Language Models Reliable Argument Quality Annotators?
finding: GPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 rated 15 Dagstuhl quality dimensions (incl. local acceptability, relevance, sufficiency). The models agree with each other and with humans more than humans agree among themselves.
numbers: Dagstuhl-15512 corpus, 320 args, 304 kept; 3 experts, 108 novices. Human overall alpha 0.37 (novices), 0.40 (experts); best single-dimension human alpha 0.43-0.45. LLM run-to-run alpha: GPT-3.5 0.73-0.78; PaLM 2 0.98-0.99 without reasoning, 0.76-0.78 with reasoning. Human-LLM peak 0.71 (PaLM 2, appropriateness and global relevance).
limits: Old models (GPT-3.5-0613, PaLM 2). PaLM 2 gave no score in about 23% of cases (content policy). Authors say that using repeated runs as stand-in annotators is unproven.
agent_relevance: High LLM self-consistency is not validity. A Verify checklist built on ARS scores will be stable but may be stable and wrong.

source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Are Large Language Models Reliable Argument Quality Annotators? (adding LLM votes)
finding: Adding LLM annotations to human panels changes agreement, and the sign depends on the model.
numbers: Adding 5 PaLM 2 annotations raised expert alpha from 0.40 to 0.50 and novice alpha from 0.37 to 0.45 (p<0.05). Adding GPT-3.5 annotations significantly lowered agreement.
limits: Agreement is not accuracy; there is no ground truth for argument quality. Reasoning prompts lowered PaLM 2 consistency (0.98-0.99 to 0.76-0.78).
agent_relevance: Do not assume one judge model is safe as a Verify voter; test its agreement first (G4, G5).

source: Dhole, Shu, Agichtein (2024) ConQRet: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Argumentation with LLM Judges
finding: Pointwise GPT-3.5 judging of the Dagstuhl dimensions (setup from Mirzakhmedova) is erratic per dimension. Listwise judging plus self-consistency and a stronger model raises expert agreement.
numbers: Expert vs LLM Krippendorff alpha on ArgQuality (320 args, 15 dims): GPT-3.5 pointwise ranges from -0.40 to 0.64 across dimensions. GPT-3.5 listwise 0.13-0.36 on most dims; listwise+self-consistency (SC) about 0.34 overall and 0.35 average quality; GPT-4o listwise+SC 0.48 overall and 0.48 average quality, 0.31-0.57 per dimension.
limits: Table read from PDF text; column order inferred. Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o on this corpus. Agreement is with 3 experts, not ground truth.
agent_relevance: Per-dimension judge scores are very noisy for weak models. Use a strong model and several samples when scoring acceptability, relevance, sufficiency.

source: Dhole, Shu, Agichtein (2024) ConQRet: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Argumentation with LLM Judges (order and shots)
finding: Changing the order of the 15 quality dimensions inside one prompt changes the scores a lot; averaging three runs fixes most of it. Zero-shot beat few-shot.
numbers: Mean rating over 3 runs gives high agreement for overall and average quality at the cost of 2 extra inference calls. Small phi-3 models (7B, 14B) failed to follow the rubric (missing values, bad JSON).
limits: Reported through appendix tables; no single headline number. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Rubric item order is a nuisance variable. Randomize or average over item order when the agent scores A, R and S together.

source: Dhole, Shu, Agichtein (2024) ConQRet: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Argumentation with LLM Judges (retrieval-augmented argument judging)
finding: Asking the judge to first score retrieval metrics (context relevance, groundedness) and then argument quality improves agreement with humans on retrieval-augmented arguments.
numbers: ConQRet: 73 long human-authored arguments over 10 topics. Krippendorff alpha human vs GPT-4o listwise: no RAG metrics 0.184; plus RAG metrics 0.395; plus fine-grained document-level RAG metrics 0.428; with SC majority 0.461. Fine-grained context relevance tracked true precision (0.505 true vs 0.548 predicted at 0% noise). The direct single-score metric stayed 0.82-0.92 regardless of 0-70% irrelevant context.
limits: Small benchmark (73 args). Judge is GPT-4o; gold is a few expert raters.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a staged Verify: score relevance of each piece of evidence first, then sufficiency of the whole. A single holistic score does not notice irrelevant evidence.

source: Ocampo, Nyiranziza, Ceolin (2026) Argument Quality Assessment with Large Language Models: A Pairwise Bradley-Terry Approach
finding: 12 open LLMs x 3 prompt styles (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) judged argument pairs on logical, rhetorical and dialectic quality (logic covers acceptability, relevance, sufficiency). Best agreement with humans is only moderate.
numbers: 36 configs. Best: Llama-70B few-shot, Pearson 0.473, Spearman 0.477, Kendall 0.327 vs human Bradley-Terry scores; Cohen kappa 0.493, 52.93% pair agreement; MAE 0.811, RMSE 1.027. Qwen2.5-72B zero-shot next: 0.463/0.466/0.319. Run to run: at most 7.75% of pairs got different labels over 3 runs.
limits: Pairwise task, not per-premise ARS scoring. Weak models gave near-zero or negative correlations.
agent_relevance: Pairwise comparison of two candidate answers by a 70B model is only moderately aligned with humans. Do not use one judge call as a pass/fail gate.

source: Ocampo, Nyiranziza, Ceolin (2026) Argument Quality Assessment with Large Language Models: A Pairwise Bradley-Terry Approach (prompt and size effects)
finding: No prompt style wins everywhere. Chain-of-thought often lowered agreement. Few-shot helped only the large models. Bigger is not always better.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: CoT Pearson 0.402 but few-shot -0.047 and zero-shot 0.093. Llama-8B zero-shot Pearson -0.034, CoT 0.354. Few-shot hurt most medium models except Mixtral; helped Llama-70B and Command-R-104B. Mistral-7B beat Mistral-22B. The three dimensions were about equally hard.
limits: One dataset, three runs per cell.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'think step by step' improves argument evaluation. Test per judge model at equal tokens (G7).

source: Ocampo, Nyiranziza, Ceolin (2026) Argument Quality Assessment with Large Language Models: A Pairwise Bradley-Terry Approach (judge to judge)
finding: LLM judges agree with each other (Llama-70B zero-shot vs its own few-shot) far more than with humans.
numbers: Llama-70B zero-shot vs its few-shot version: Pearson 0.892, Spearman 0.892, Kendall 0.718, kappa 0.831, 84.45% agreement. Against humans kappa is 0.493.
limits: Shows a shared view among model runs, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Support for G4: model agreement is a hint, not proof. ARS verdicts from the same model family are correlated.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis
finding: Uses Govier's ARG conditions (acceptable, relevant, good grounds/sufficient) with Walton critical questions to score nine frontier models defending moral verdicts. Models almost always pass acceptability and relevance. Failures sit in grounds and sufficiency.
numbers: 9 models, 200 MoralChoice items, 6,778 judge-scored cells (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 as judges). Local and global relevance failure under 0.5% on every model. Failure (criterion not met) in 18.2% of cells; two outliers (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3) hold 67.8% of failures. Claude: 51.1% global sufficiency fail, 22.5% local grounds fail. Llama 3.3: 46.9% local grounds, 29.8% global sufficiency.
limits: Moral dilemmas only; judges are LLMs; rubric is ternary (1-3). Claude is both a judge and the outlier subject; self-preference not tested.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency, not acceptability or relevance, is the weak spot to check in a Verify step.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (judge validation)
finding: Two LLM judges agree on the binary 'criterion not met' flag 89.6% of the time. Disagreements were resolved by humans.
numbers: 3,389 paired cells, 352 disagreements. Critical question generation (phase 2) done by a single judge.
limits: Binary agreement is inflated when failures are rare (18.2%).
agent_relevance: A binary ARS fail flag is judgeable at about 90% two-judge agreement. Partial scores are less reliable.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (what failure looks like)
finding: Low-grounds answers are not longer. They hedge more with epistemic modal verbs. Models under-commit rather than contradict themselves.
numbers: Median words 738 (low grounds, n=591) vs 767 (high grounds, n=999). Commitment stability correlates with local grounds (Spearman 0.27) and global sufficiency (0.49). Only 2.1% of cells hit the minimum commitment score. All 144 self-contradictions co-occur with global sufficiency failure but are only 12.4% of local grounds failures.
limits: Correlational; lexicon-based hedge counts.
agent_relevance: Hedging is a cheap, code-checkable proxy for weak grounds. Length is not.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (reasoning vs justification)
finding: Models defend their reasoning trace better than their post-hoc justification on every Govier dimension except saturated local relevance. They also name a different Walton scheme in about 20% of dilemmas.
numbers: 3,182 paired observations, 8 models (GPT-5.4 excluded, reasoning encrypted). Every model has a positive local-mean advantage for reasoning; 6 of 8 a significant global advantage; largest gaps +0.032 (Qwen 3.6 Plus, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Value-based practical reasoning is about 72% of reasoning-track and 67% of justification-track schemes.
limits: Effect sizes are small (0.03 on a 0-1 scale).
agent_relevance: A justification written after the verdict is weaker than the reasoning. Judge the actual reasoning (G2), not the story told afterwards.

source: Deshpande et al. (2023) Contextualizing Argument Quality Assessment with Relevant Knowledge (SPARK)
finding: Adding LLM-generated feedback, assumptions, a similar-quality argument and a counter-argument to a dual BERT scorer improves prediction of cogency (which covers ARS).
numbers: GAQCorpus test, Spearman: cogency 0.3480 (BERT) to 0.4242 (SPARK all four); effectiveness 0.2804 to 0.4513; reasonableness 0.3285 to 0.4135. Single augmentations, cogency: feedback 0.4184, counter-argument 0.4030, similar quality 0.4059, assumptions only 0.3699. GPT-3.5 zero-shot cogency 0.2879.
limits: Zero-shot IBM-30K: feedback-only 0.2742 beat all four 0.2238, and GPT-3.5 alone beat SPARK there (0.2698). Smaller generators gave weaker gains. Authors note GPT-3.5 hallucination. Table and text disagree in places.
agent_relevance: Counter-argument and feedback generation help a cogency score more than listing assumptions. Supports a critic-then-score design where the critic text is evidence for code to use.

source: Liu, Feng, Chang (2024) CASA: Causality-driven Argument Sufficiency Assessment
finding: Zero-shot sufficiency check using a causal 'probability of sufficiency'. The LLM writes contexts where premise and conclusion are both absent, injects the premise, then asks whether the conclusion follows. Beats direct prompting.
numbers: BIG-bench logical fallacy detection: CASA (Llama-2-7B) accuracy 79.0 / macro-F1 73.4 vs zero-shot prompting 70.0 / 66.8 and one-shot 74.1 / 68.6. TULU-7B: 77.0/70.8 vs 59.5/59.3. Climate fallacy set (30 correct, 76 fallacious): CASA 67.9/61.2 vs 51.9/48.0 zero-shot. Removing the intervention step: macro-F1 73.4 to 65.8. Step-wise human check: all aspects above 90%.
limits: Only 7B models (GPT-4 avoided over data contamination). Climate set is small. Sufficiency labels are subjective: in Wachsmuth 2017 the three best annotators reached alpha 0.28.
agent_relevance: A counterfactual probe 'could the conclusion fail even if the premise holds?' is a concrete S8 test for sufficiency. About 10 points over direct prompting at 7B.

source: Liu, Feng, Chang (2024) CASA: Causality-driven Argument Sufficiency Assessment (writing help)
finding: Objections CASA generates for insufficient arguments in student essays were judged more rational and feasible than directly prompted objections. Revisions based on them were more often judged better.
numbers: 100 random arguments from the AAE essay corpus, 3 annotators, revised vs original comparison after GPT-4 revision.
limits: Small human study; GPT-4 did the revision itself.
agent_relevance: Generating the strongest objection to the premises is a usable repair signal for G2-style revision.

source: Gurcke, Alshomary, Wachsmuth (2021) Assessing the Sufficiency of Arguments through Conclusion Generation
finding: Test: can the conclusion of a sufficient argument be generated from its premises? Generated conclusions did not help the classifier, and a premises-only classifier already matches the best score.
numbers: Stab & Gurevych essays: RoBERTa premises+conclusion macro-F1 .885 (acc .896); premises-only .875; conclusion-only .553; generated-conclusion-only .532; CNN baseline .831; human upper bound .883 (433 args, 3 annotators).
limits: Shows a dataset shortcut: sufficiency labels are predictable from premises alone, so 'solved on the corpus' does not mean the models check the premise-conclusion link.
agent_relevance: Warning: a model may rate sufficiency from surface features of the premises, not the link to the claim. Test with swapped conclusions (G3).

source: Stab and Gurevych (2017) Recognizing Insufficiently Supported Arguments in Argumentative Essays (read from the paper text)
finding: First model for insufficiency in essays. A CNN gets near but below the human upper bound.
numbers: Essay corpus 402 essays / 1,029 arguments. CNN macro-F1 about .827 vs human upper bound macro-F1 .887 (accuracy .911; 433 args, 3 annotators). Overall alpha 0.77, but agreement on instances where an annotator flags insufficiency (32% of instances) is much lower (per Liu 2024 footnote).
limits: Only parts of the paper were read; table rows were partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Sets the human ceiling (about .88 F1) that LLM sufficiency checks are compared to.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017) Argumentation Quality Assessment: Theory vs. Practice
finding: Crowd (lay) ratings of the theory-based dimensions agree weakly with experts. Local sufficiency is the weakest of the three ARS dimensions.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha crowd vs expert (mean of ratings): local acceptability 0.49, local relevance 0.42, local sufficiency 0.18, cogency 0.27. With MACE aggregation: 0.35, 0.39, 0.31, 0.38. 102 crowd annotators.
limits: Different aggregation changes the ranking of dimensions. Human ceiling is low.
agent_relevance: Sets the human baseline: even people agree poorly on sufficiency, so LLM-human agreement near 0.4 is near the ceiling.

source: Wachsmuth, Lapesa, Cabrio, Lauscher, Park, Vecchi, Villata, Ziegenbein (2024) Argument Quality Assessment in the Age of Instruction-Following LLMs
finding: Position paper: argument quality has too many notions and is perceived subjectively. LLMs should be instructed with argumentation theory, not only fine-tuned for leaderboards.
numbers: Survey of the 15-dimension taxonomy; no experiments.
limits: Opinion paper without measurements; skimmed.
agent_relevance: Argues for theory-grounded prompting (ARS definitions in the prompt) but gives no measured gain.

source: Romberg, Maurer, Wachsmuth, Lapesa (2025) Towards a Perspectivist Turn in Argument Quality Assessment
finding: Review of 103 argument quality datasets. Only 24 keep non-aggregated annotations. Annotator information is rarely reported. Plea for modelling several valid perspectives.
numbers: 103 datasets surveyed, 24 non-aggregated; annotator information reported for only 8 datasets (text excerpt).
limits: Pilot study is small; focus is datasets, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Ground truth for 'sufficient' is partly subjective. The agent should give a graded verdict with reasons, not claim certainty.

source: Sternlicht, Gera, Bar-Haim, Hope, Slonim (2025) Debatable Intelligence: Benchmarking LLM Judges via Debate Speech Evaluation
finding: On 600+ debate speeches with 15 human raters each, big LLM judges match or beat single-human agreement but behave differently: they give lower scores yet rank speeches similarly.
numbers: Models under 7B fail; Qwen2.5-72B exceeds human-human kappa. GPT-4.1 speeches were rated above human expert debaters. Pearson of mean score per speech source, human vs LLM: Llama-3.3-70B CoT 0.85, Qwen-2.5-32B CoT 0.92, o3-mini 0.89, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 0.88, GPT-4.1-mini CoT 0.91. CoT slightly helps larger models and hurts some small ones; o3 underperformed.
limits: Whole-speech quality, not the ARS criteria. Crowd raters.
agent_relevance: Relative ranking by a strong judge is reliable; absolute scores are shifted. Compare candidates, do not threshold.

source: Sternlicht, Gera, Bar-Haim, Hope, Slonim (2025) Debatable Intelligence: Benchmarking LLM Judges via Debate Speech Evaluation (size effect)
finding: Model size matters sharply: small models are near random, with a jump around 7B.
numbers: Pearson of per-source mean score with humans, Qwen2.5 family: 0.5B -0.25, 1.5B 0.13, 3B 0.06, 7B 0.7, 14B 0.86, 32B 0.91, 72B 0.87 (read from figure text; approximate).
limits: Figure values read from rendered chart text.
agent_relevance: A weak local judge is worse than none. Keep the Verify judge strong or use code checks.

source: Payandeh et al. (2024) How susceptible are LLMs to Logical Fallacies? (LOGICOM)
finding: In multi-round debates, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 debaters are persuaded more often by fallacious arguments than by logical ones. The stronger model is more susceptible.
numbers: 200 claims x 3 scenarios x 3 repeats = 1,800 debates. Convinced: GPT-3.5 17% of fallacy debates vs 10% logical; GPT-4 56% vs 37%. Relative: 41% (GPT-3.5) and 69% (GPT-4) more likely to be convinced by fallacies. In the other analysis, 37% vs 29% (GPT-3.5) and 67% vs 37% (GPT-4). Opinion moved from disagree to agree in 16.13% (GPT-3.5) and 20.25% (GPT-4) of cases.
limits: Persuader is GPT-3.5 for both; moderator is PaLM; claims have no ground truth; stance change is not necessarily error.
agent_relevance: Models do not reliably check relevance and sufficiency of premises. A Verify step needs an explicit ARS or fallacy check when the agent faces persuasive input.

source: Lim and Perrault (2024) Evaluation of an LLM in Identifying Logical Fallacies: A Call for Rigor When Adopting LLMs in HCI Research
finding: GPT-4 with a 3-shot prompt labels 7 fallacy types in short texts at 0.79 accuracy overall. The 0.90 figure excludes 'None' outputs.
numbers: LOGIC dataset (2,449 items, 13 types), N=780: accuracy 0.79, macro-F1 0.71 (precision 0.76, recall 0.66); subset N=685: accuracy 0.90, F1 0.88. Appeal to Emotion returned None for 16 of 41 (about 39%). Against the Person 0.94 on subset. 12% of Appeal to Emotion labeled Red Herring.
limits: Seven of 300+ fallacies; mostly 1-2 sentence texts; GPT-4 only; prompt tuned by the authors.
agent_relevance: Most errors were misses, not wrong labels: the model fails to see a flaw. A checklist should push the model to look for one.

source: Calvo Figueras and Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation: A Challenging Reasoning Task for LLMs
finding: Eleven LLMs generate Walton-style critical questions (the questions that probe acceptability, relevance and sufficiency of a scheme). None exceeds 57% useful questions zero-shot.
numbers: About 5K manually annotated questions; labels Useful / Unhelpful / Invalid; annotator agreement 0.54 in the final round. Test-set reference questions 42.68% Useful. Averages over 3 evaluators: gemma-2-27b 54.03, Llama-3-70B 53.52, Qwen2.5-72B 52.71; claude-3-5-sonnet best overall. Task-specific systems in the shared task reached nearly 10 points more. Reference-based LLM judge ranking correlates with human ranking at Pearson 0.86 (Claude) and 0.80 (Gemma); direct LLM labeling never exceeded moderate agreement.
limits: Evaluation depends on the judge (different winners: gpt-4o, claude-3-5-sonnet, Qwen2.5-VL-72B). Qwen and Claude produce formulaic template questions (least diverse).
agent_relevance: Critical-question generation is hard for models. They often output generic 'what evidence supports the claim?' questions, a weak check.

source: Calvo Figueras and Agerri (2024) Critical Questions Generation: Motivation and Challenges
finding: Proposes generating critical questions from an argumentative text, built from Walton templates plus LLM prompting. LLMs are reasonable generators but have room for improvement.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract (only the abstract was opened).
limits: Abstract only; do not rely on numbers.
agent_relevance: Source for using scheme-specific questions as the check list.

source: Johnson and Blair (2006) Logical Self-Defense; Govier (2010) A Practical Study of Argument
finding: Original statement of the ARS (acceptability, relevance, sufficiency) criteria. Not opened this session; citations only.
numbers: None collected.
limits: Books; definitions reached only through secondary papers above (Wachsmuth 2017, Henselmans 2026).
agent_relevance: The three tests are the checklist used by every LLM study above. The empirical evidence is about models, not about the criteria themselves.

source: Al Rebdawi and Alhamzeh (2025) Argument Quality Annotation and Gender Bias Detection in Financial Communication through LLMs
finding: GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 and Gemma 2 annotated financial argument quality (strength, specificity, persuasiveness, objectivity) more consistently than humans. An injected gender cue shifted ratings.
numbers: At temperature 0.3, GPT-4o run-to-run agreement 83-90% (text). Model size did not predict consistency (Gemma 2, the smallest, matched GPT-4o). Fleiss kappa tables could not be parsed reliably, so not recorded.
limits: Not the ARS criteria; kappa tables garbled in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant cues (speaker gender) can move quality scores. Add a relevance filter before scoring.
